Never, on any timescale that matters. The premise is a myth.

Glass at room temperature is an amorphous solid, not a liquid. Zanotto (1998) estimated the viscosity of medieval cathedral glass at room temperature at roughly 10^41 Pa·s or more. At that viscosity, visible flow would take far longer than the age of the universe. A later estimate (Zanotto & Gupta, 2017) for window glass put relaxation times at around 10^32 years. Your windows will break, cloud, or have their seals fail long before any sag appears.

Old church panes are uneven because of how they were made. Crown and cylinder glass came out with inconsistent thickness, and glaziers often set the thicker edge at the bottom for stability. Some old panes, though, are thicker at the top or sides, which flow couldn't explain. Roman glassware and centuries-old telescope lenses also show no measurable flow.

If your windows do look distorted, the likely causes are frame settling, failed double-glazing seals (fogging), or ordinary manufacturing waviness, not the glass flowing.
